In 2023 *The Economist* published a way of talking about the climate cost of food that is
easy to remember. Instead of reporting grams of CO₂, they express everything in **bananas**:
how many times more carbon does a kilogram of this food emit than a kilogram of bananas?

They computed the index three ways, because "a kilogram of lettuce" and "a kilogram of beef"
are not the same amount of food at all. They ranked the foods per kilogram, per thousand
calories, and per hundred grams of protein. The three rankings disagree with each other, and
working out why they disagree is most of this practice.

Today you will rank this dataset all three ways yourself, and then work out what the
disagreements between your three rankings actually mean.

:::{.callout-note title="Reference"}
The Economist and Solstad, S., 2023. The Economist's Banana index. First published in the
article "A different way to measure the climate impact of food", *The Economist*, April 11,
2023. The data are [posted on GitHub](https://github.com/TheEconomist/banana-index-data).
:::

## Today's two patterns

Every code cell in this practice is built from one of these two patterns, so you should not
need to look them up more than once.

```python
df[df['column'] > value]                             # the filter pattern
df.sort_values('column', ascending=False).head(n)    # the top-N pattern
```

## Setup

1. Create a new notebook named `EOD_Day3_Banana_Index.ipynb`.

2. Add a title cell:

```markdown

Date: 09/02/2026
```

3. Read the data, using `entity` as the index. The `entity` column holds the food names, and
   making it the index means every ranking you print will be labelled with food names instead
   of row numbers.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/banana_index.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url, index_col='entity')
df.shape
```

4. The file has five columns that are bookkeeping rather than data: `year`,
   `Banana values`, `type`, `Chart?`, and `Unnamed: 16`. Remove them.

:::{.callout-tip title="🧭 Field Note: dropping columns you don't want"}
`.drop()` takes a **list** of column names and `axis='columns'`, and returns a new DataFrame
without them. Here is the whole line. Run it as written:

```python
df = df.drop(['year', 'Banana values', 'type', 'Chart?', 'Unnamed: 16'], axis='columns')
```

There are two things worth noticing here. The names go in a list, exactly like the lists you
used to select columns yesterday. And `axis='columns'` tells pandas that you mean columns and
not rows, because `.drop()` can remove either one.

📖 [Cheatsheet: pandas DataFrames](../cheatsheets/pandas_dataframes.qmd)
:::

```{python}
df = df.drop(['year', 'Banana values', 'type', 'Chart?', 'Unnamed: 16'], axis='columns')
df.columns.tolist()
```

## Part 4: Filtering by score

Now use the other one, the filter pattern.

11. Use the filter pattern to find every food with a `Bananas index (kg)` above 10. How many
    are there?

```{python}
expensive_by_weight = df[df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 10]
expensive_by_weight.shape
```

12. Use `~` to find the foods that are **not** above a score of 1 on `Bananas index (kg)`,
    that is, foods no worse than a banana by weight. How many are there?

13. Now filter for `Bananas index (kg)` **below** 1 instead. You should get a different number
    from the one you got in question 12. Explain the difference in one sentence.

```{python}
no_worse_than_banana = df[~(df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 1)]
print(no_worse_than_banana.shape)

better_than_banana = df[df['Bananas index (kg)'] < 1]
print(better_than_banana.shape)
```

14. Use a **two-condition** filter to find the foods that score above 5 per kilogram **and**
    below 1 per 100 g of protein. End the line with `.copy()`, because you will display the
    result a couple of different ways. Display the two banana index columns for those foods,
    ranked by `Bananas index (kg)`.

```{python}
costly_but_protein_rich = df[
    (df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 5) & (df['Bananas index (100g protein)'] < 1)
].copy()

print(costly_but_protein_rich.shape)

costly_but_protein_rich[
    ['Bananas index (kg)', 'Bananas index (100g protein)']
].sort_values('Bananas index (kg)', ascending=False)
```

## Part 5: Land, not carbon

The banana index columns are all about emissions. The dataset also has a land use column,
`land_use_1000kcal`, which gives square metres of land per thousand calories.

16. Use `.loc[]` to look up the value of `land_use_1000kcal` for `Bananas`.
17. Use the top-N pattern to display the 10 foods with the highest `land_use_1000kcal`.
18. Use `.idxmax()` on `land_use_1000kcal` to get the name of the single most land-hungry food.
    Then use two `.loc[]` lookups and a division to work out how many times more land that
    food needs than bananas do.

```{python}
banana_land_use = df.loc['Bananas', 'land_use_1000kcal']
banana_land_use
```

```{python}
df['land_use_1000kcal'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

```{python}
hungriest = df['land_use_1000kcal'].idxmax()
print(hungriest)
print(df.loc[hungriest, 'land_use_1000kcal'] / df.loc['Bananas', 'land_use_1000kcal'])
```

## Part 6: Cheese

The dataset has a lot of cheese in it. Cheese is worth a section of its own, because it is the
one dairy product that shows up alongside meat at the top of the emissions rankings.

20. Build a table of just the cheeses, then find the cheese with the highest
    `Bananas index (1000 kcalories)`.

:::{.callout-tip title="🧭 Field Note: selecting rows whose label contains a word"}
The food names are the **index** of your table rather than a column, so the filter pattern
will not work on them. `.filter()` will. Given a substring, it keeps every row whose label
contains that substring:

```python
cheese = df.filter(like='heese', axis='rows')
```

We use `like='heese'` rather than `'cheese'` so that both `Cheddar cheese` and `Cheesecake`
match, whatever their capitalisation. Run the line as written, then rank `cheese` with the
top-N pattern exactly as you have been doing all along.

📖 [Cheatsheet: data selection and filtering](../cheatsheets/data_selection.qmd)
:::

```{python}
cheese = df.filter(like='heese', axis='rows')
print(cheese.shape)

cheese['Bananas index (1000 kcalories)'].sort_values(ascending=False)
```

    rows on text.

## The grammar minute

Look back through your notebook. Almost every code cell you wrote was one of two
patterns:

```python
df[df['column'] > value]                             # filter: fewer rows
df.sort_values('column', ascending=False).head(n)    # rank: same rows, new order, first few
```

Everything else was a variation. `&` and `|` joined two questions into one filter. `~` turned
a question around. `.idxmax()` returned the label instead of the row. `.loc[]` looked up one
value.

Two patterns got you through every question in this document. You will be writing both of
them nearly every day for the rest of the course.
